title: Why watch ads show 10:10 (and why we show 10:04)

slides.title: Why does every watch ad say *10:10?*
slides.body: Next time you see a watch ad, check the time. It's almost always ten past ten. Here's why.

slides.title: It *frames* the logo
slides.body: The hands form a neat V and **leave the brand name under the 12 uncovered**, along with the date window and subdials.

slides.title: It looks like a *smile*
slides.body: In a 2017 study, watches set to 10:10 **made people feel happier and more likely to buy.** Watches set to 8:20, a “frown”, had no such effect.

slides.title: It wasn't always *10:10*
slides.body: Early ads often used **8:20**: just as symmetrical, but sad-looking. By the 1950s, brands had switched to 10:10, and it stuck.

slides.title: No, it's not about a *famous death*
slides.body: A popular story says 10:10 marks the moment Lincoln or JFK died. **False.** Lincoln was shot around 10:15 p.m. but died at 7:22 a.m. JFK was declared dead at 1:00 p.m.

slides.title: So why does our clock say *10:04?*
slides.body: Because on November 12, 1955, lightning struck a certain clock tower in Hill Valley. **Our logo stops at the moment that bolt sent Marty back to the future.**

slides.title: This is *Time Circuits*
slides.body: Every week we set the dials to a different moment in watch history: **inventions, legendary brands and the watches of the big screen.**

caption:
Almost every watch ad shows 10:10. Ours shows 10:04. 🕙⚡

10:10 frames the logo and looks like a smile, and a 2017 study found it actually makes people want to buy. 10:04 is when lightning struck the Hill Valley clock tower. Welcome to Time Circuits: the stories behind the watches that shaped history.
